title: Undecidability
body:
The edge of the ladder. [[Turing Machine]] gives the strongest machine there is, and this is
the proof that even it cannot answer some questions. Not "we have not found the algorithm
yet": no algorithm exists, and never will, whatever hardware you buy.

[[Turing Machine]] holds the machine model, the decidable/recognisable split, and the
Church-Turing thesis. This note is the argument itself.

## The vocabulary

| Term | Means |
|---|---|
| **Decidable** | some TM halts on every input and answers correctly |
| **Recognisable** | some TM accepts every string in $L$, but may loop forever on strings not in $L$ |
| **Undecidable** | no TM decides it; it may still be recognisable |

Every decidable language is recognisable. The reverse fails, and the gap between the two rows
is where all of this lives.

## Why something has to be undecidable

The counting argument, before any specific problem:

- A Turing machine can be written as a finite string, so there are **countably many** machines.
- A language is a subset of $\Sigma^*$, and there are **uncountably many** of those, by
  Cantor's diagonal argument.

Countably many machines, uncountably many languages. Almost every language has no machine at
all. The halting problem is just the first *natural* example, not a rare one.

## The halting problem

> $HALT = \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ halts on } w\}$ is undecidable.

A [[Proof By Contradiction]], and the proof is short enough to reconstruct from scratch.

1. Suppose a machine $H$ decides it: $H(\langle M, w\rangle)$ always halts, answering *yes* if
   $M$ halts on $w$ and *no* otherwise.
2. Build $D$, which takes a machine description $\langle M \rangle$ and does this:
   - run $H(\langle M, M\rangle)$, asking whether $M$ halts when fed its own description
   - if $H$ says *halts*, then **loop forever**
   - if $H$ says *loops*, then **halt**
   
   $D$ does the opposite of whatever $H$ predicts.
3. Now run $D$ on its own description, $D(\langle D \rangle)$.
   - If $D$ halts on $\langle D \rangle$, then $H$ said *halts*, so $D$ loops. Contradiction.
   - If $D$ loops on $\langle D \rangle$, then $H$ said *loops*, so $D$ halts. Contradiction.
4. Both branches are impossible, so $H$ does not exist. $\blacksquare$

Two ingredients make it work, and both come from the universal machine in
[[Turing Machine]]: a program can be **data** (so $M$ can be fed to itself), and a program can
**negate** what it is told. That is the same self-reference as "this sentence is false", made
mechanical.

$A_{TM} = \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w\}$ is the usual companion result:
recognisable but not decidable. Simulating $M$ on $w$ works fine if $M$ accepts; if it loops
you wait forever and never get to say no.

## Reduction

Nobody re-runs diagonalisation for each new problem. Instead, show that solving your problem
would let you solve the halting problem:

> If $A$ reduces to $B$ and $A$ is undecidable, then $B$ is undecidable.

Get the direction right. You reduce the **known-undecidable** problem *to* the new one, so a
decider for $B$ would give you one for $A$, which you know cannot exist. (This is the same
machinery as [[NP-Complete]] reductions, used to prove impossibility rather than hardness.)

Undecidable by reduction:

- Does $M$ accept *any* string? Does it accept *all* strings?
- Do two machines recognise the same language?
- Is a given [[Context-Free Grammars|CFG]] ambiguous?
- Do two CFGs generate the same language?
- The Post correspondence problem.
- **Rice's theorem**, which generalises the lot: *every* non-trivial property of the language a
  machine recognises is undecidable. Trivial means true of all machines or of none.

## What it means in practice

You use undecidable problems constantly, because impossible-in-general is not
impossible-in-every-case:

- Compilers cannot detect all infinite loops, so they warn about the cases they can see.
- Static analysers and type checkers are deliberately conservative: they reject some safe
  programs rather than promise an answer they cannot deliver.
- Perfect virus detection by behaviour is undecidable, which is why antivirus uses signatures
  and heuristics.
- Termination checkers work on restricted languages where the question becomes decidable again.

The move is always the same: give up completeness, or shrink the language.

## Relatives

[[Godel's Theorem]] is the same self-reference in logic: any consistent system strong enough
for arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove. Gödel got there in 1931, Turing in 1936,
and the halting problem gives a shorter proof of Gödel's result.

Note the distinction from [[NP-Complete]]: undecidable means *no algorithm exists*;
NP-complete means an algorithm exists but is probably slow. Different kinds of bad.

## Core Facts to Know

- **Decidable**: a TM halts on every input. **Recognisable**: a TM accepts every string in $L$, may loop otherwise.
- Every decidable language is recognisable; the converse is false.
- $L$ is decidable iff both $L$ and its complement are recognisable.
- Most languages are undecidable by counting: countably many machines, uncountably many languages.
- The **halting problem** is undecidable.
- The proof is [[Proof By Contradiction]] via self-reference: build $D$ that does the opposite of the prediction, then run it on itself.
- It needs the universal machine: programs are data.
- $A_{TM}$ is recognisable but not decidable.
- To prove a new problem undecidable, **reduce a known undecidable problem to it**.
- **Rice's theorem**: every non-trivial property of a machine's language is undecidable.
- Equivalence of two CFGs and ambiguity of a CFG are both undecidable.
- Undecidable ≠ [[NP-Complete]]: no algorithm at all, versus an algorithm that is too slow.
- Same self-reference as [[Godel's Theorem]].

Added 2026-08-16 from [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]]: the escape-time algorithm for the
[[Mandelbrot Set]] is a worked example of the recognisable-but-not-decidable distinction, and a
rare visual one. If the orbit passes $|z| > 2$ you have **proved** the point is outside and you
halt; if it never does you never learn that, so you cut off at an iteration limit and guess. The
black region of every Mandelbrot picture is that guess.
